explanation: Double-quoted strings are parsed for variable interpolation and escape sequences, while single-quoted strings are treated almost literally, so they are processed differently.
The null coalescing operator (??) uses isset() semantics, so it does not emit a notice or warning when the variable is undefined.
echo with comma-separated arguments outputs them in sequence, so 'a' followed by 'b' prints 'ab'.
print is a language construct that always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions.
The ?: operator returns its left operand when it is truthy, not falsy; it returns the right operand when the left is falsy.
PHP 8 moved the concatenation operator's precedence below addition and subtraction, so '1 . 2 + 3' now evaluates as '1 . (2 + 3)'.
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so it evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
In PHP 8, '.' and '+' have equal precedence and are left-associative, so it evaluates ('sum: ' . 2) + 3, and adding 3 to the non-numeric string 'sum: 2' throws a TypeError.
Strict comparison (===) requires identical key/value pairs in the same order and with the same types, so element order matters.
The == operator is a loose (not strict) comparison, and 0 == false evaluates to true because false is converted to 0.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number converts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 evaluates to false (unlike PHP 7, where it was true).
In PHP's loose comparison, null == 0, null == "", and null == false all evaluate to true.
Casting a string to int in PHP extracts the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
In PHP, the arithmetic + operator converts the numeric string '5' to the integer 5, so the result is 10.
When cast to string, false becomes an empty string "", while true becomes "1".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly identical to 0.3.
strrev() reverses bytes, not characters, so multibyte UTF-8 sequences are broken and the result is corrupted.
str_contains() checks if the haystack contains the needle, and 'Hello world' does contain 'world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right (default), left, or both sides via its optional pad_type argument.
By default trim() strips whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen() counts bytes, and 'é' occupies 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 5 characters equal 6 bytes.
A negative start of -3 counts three characters back from the end, returning the last three characters 'def'.
PHP strings are immutable; ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased rather than modifying the original.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) parses variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') treats everything literally like single quotes.
sort() reindexes the array with numeric keys starting at 0, so it does not preserve key-to-value associations (unlike asort()).
PHP automatically casts string keys containing valid decimal integers (like '5') to integer keys.
By default in_array() uses loose (==) comparison; strict comparison is enabled only when the third parameter is set to true.
When called without a callback, array_filter() removes all elements that evaluate to false (e.g., 0, "", null, false, []).
By default, array_slice() reindexes numeric keys; keys are only preserved when the fifth parameter preserve_keys is set to true.
array_slice starts at offset 1 and takes 2 elements, returning [20, 30].
The + union operator keeps keys from the left array ('a' => 1) and adds only new keys from the right ('b' => 2), giving 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for unpacking arrays with string keys using the spread operator, which previously only worked with integer keys.
Since PHP 8.1, named arguments can be combined with argument unpacking in a single call, e.g. foo(...$args, name: 'x').
Anonymous functions in PHP do not automatically inherit outer scope variables; they must be explicitly imported with the `use` keyword (or arrow functions, which auto-capture).
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function at call time, regardless of the declared parameters.
PHP arrow functions (fn) must contain exactly one expression after => and cannot have a block body with curly braces.
Arrow functions capture outer variables automatically by value, not by reference.
A closure declared with the static keyword cannot automatically bind $this, so using $this inside it would result in an error.
The closure captured $x by value at creation time, so later changes to $x don't affect it.
In weak typing mode, numeric strings like "5" are automatically coerced to int when passed to an int parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared directly in constructor parameters.
The 'final' keyword prevents a method from being overridden in child classes.
The final keyword on a method prevents subclasses from overriding it.
Private members are only accessible within the class that declares them; subclasses must use protected or public visibility instead.
PHP generates anonymous class names in the form 'class@anonymous\0/path/file.php:line$index', so the segment before the NUL byte is 'class@anonymous'.
Private methods are not inherited by child classes, so a child can declare a method with the same name freely, including with different visibility.
__get() is called for inaccessible properties, which includes not only non-existent ones but also existing properties that are private or protected.
Modifying a readonly property after initialization throws an instance of the Error class, not Exception.
PHP interfaces may declare constants, which are inherited by classes implementing the interface.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a class or implements an interface.
Since PHP 5.3, interfaces may declare static methods, which implementing classes must define as static.
instanceof returns true not only for class inheritance but also when the object implements the given interface.
PHP interfaces may only declare method signatures (and constants); they cannot provide method bodies, unlike traits.
In PHP, abstract methods may be declared public, protected, or (since PHP 7.1) private visibility is not allowed, but protected is permitted.
cases() returns an array of all enum cases, and this enum defines three cases: A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants (but not properties-as-constants conflicting with class constants).
Since PHP 7, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface.
TypeError inherits from Error, not Exception; only Throwable (via Error|Exception or a Throwable type) can catch both.
The @ operator only suppresses errors and warnings; thrown exceptions still propagate and cannot be suppressed by it.
intdiv() throws a DivisionByZeroError (an ArithmeticError subclass) when the divisor is zero.
The finally block always executes after try/catch, whether or not an exception was thrown or caught.
An exception thrown in a finally block propagates and overrides any return value or exception from the try block.
Any object, including an Exception instance, casts to boolean true.
Shutdown functions run when script execution stops, including on exit().
The use statement is only an aliasing mechanism and does not trigger class loading; the file loads when the class is actually used (e.g., instantiated).
In PHP, `use function name` imports a function, while `use const name` imports a constant.
PSR-4 replaces the App\ prefix with src/, so the remaining namespace path maps to Controller/Api/UserController.php.
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php registers its class loader (ClassLoader) with spl_autoload_register(), making Composer classes autoloadable.
__NAMESPACE__ returns the name of the current namespace as a string (empty at global scope).
An unqualified class name is resolved relative to the current namespace (if any), not from the global root; only names with a leading backslash refer to the global namespace.
PSR-4 replaces the namespace prefix App\ with src/, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
Use statements are only allowed at the top level of a file or namespace; they cannot appear inside a function body, and imports always apply to the whole file/namespace.
In PHP, arrays (like scalars) are assigned by value, meaning the array is copied unless you explicitly assign or pass it by reference with &.
PHP arrays are assigned by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
Functions have their own local scope and cannot access global variables unless declared with global, accessed via $GLOBALS, or passed as arguments.
unset($GLOBALS['x']) actually removes the global variable entirely, including outside the function, since $GLOBALS accesses the true global scope.
The parameter is passed by reference, so incrementing $x also modifies $n.
When foreach iterates by value, it works on a (lazily) copied snapshot of the array, so modifications made to the original array during the loop do not affect the iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself, so they are shared across all instances and changes are visible in every object.
PHP array keys containing booleans are cast to integers, so true is stored as the integer key 1.
Since PHP 7, a generator can use return with a value, which is retrievable by calling getReturn() after the generator finishes.
Generators are forward-only iterators; calling rewind() on a started (fully consumed) generator throws an exception.

Calling g() returns a Generator object since the function uses yield.
The generator yields the values 1, 2, and 3 via yield from, so iterator_to_array produces a 3-element array.
SplStack implements a LIFO stack; the FIFO queue is SplQueue.
ArrayIterator wraps an array or object and allows it to be traversed using the Iterator interface.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
Since PHP 5.5, password_hash() generates a secure random salt automatically, and passing a salt manually is deprecated.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT in PHP 8 is bcrypt (password_hash with a salt), not md5; md5() never adds automatic salts.
password_verify() returns true (a boolean), and yes/no represents that boolean, since the hash correctly matches the password.
strip_tags() only removes HTML and PHP tags from a string and does nothing to prevent SQL injection; prepared statements or proper escaping are required.
Calling session_regenerate_id(true) after login generates a new session ID, preventing attackers from fixing a known session ID.
php_sapi_name() returns the name of the Server API, such as 'cli' or 'fpm-fcgi'.
session_destroy() removes the session data stored on the server, but the session cookie in the browser remains until it expires or is explicitly deleted with setcookie().
Session data is only loaded into $_SESSION after session_start() is called; without it, $_SESSION is not populated.
The array_find() function, which returns the first element matching a callback, was introduced in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing get/set logic to be defined directly in property declarations.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing separate read/write scope such as public private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5 to mark functions whose return values should not be silently discarded.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5 via the pipe operator RFC.
The clone-with syntax, clone($obj, ['x' => 1]), was introduced in PHP 8.4 via the 'clone with' RFC.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were added in PHP 8.4.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was adopted and shipped with PHP 8.5.
The clamp_v2 RFC was implemented in PHP 8.4, which introduced the clamp() function.
The Context Managers RFC (inspired by Python's 'with' statement, introducing a 'using' construct) has not been adopted into PHP; as of late 2025 it was still not part of any released PHP version.
The generics RFC was not declined in 2026; the Bound-Erased Generics proposal is still under discussion rather than formally declined.
No RFC making ZTS (threading) the default in PHP has been accepted; PHP remains non-thread-safe by default with multithreading only available in ZTS builds.
PHP 8.5 does not include generics (parameterized types); they remain a long-requested but unimplemented feature.
PHP 8.5 was released as GA on November 20, 2025, and PHP 8.6 is still in development with its GA scheduled for November 19, 2026, so as of 2026-11-07 PHP 8.5 is the latest stable version.
PHP 6 was abandoned (due to the failed Unicode/UTF-16 project), and versioning jumped from PHP 5.6 straight to PHP 7.0.
The RFC was accepted and the #[\Deprecated] attribute was added to PHP core in PHP 8.4.
In clean/onion architecture, dependencies always point inward, so inner layers have no knowledge of outer layers.
In clean/hexagonal architecture, domain entities should depend only on the language and standard library, staying independent of frameworks like Doctrine or Symfony.
Controllers and Twig templates are presentation-layer (delivery/UI) components, not part of the business-logic layer that contains use cases and domain logic.
In onion architecture, the domain model sits at the very center, surrounded by domain services, application services, and outer infrastructure layers.
Tools like deptrac analyze dependencies between layers and fail the build when a forbidden call across layer boundaries is detected.

A use case (interactor) should operate on framework-agnostic plain values (DTOs/arrays/scalars), not infrastructure details like HTTP requests or an EntityManager, to stay independent of delivery and persistence mechanisms.
A Repository provides a collection-like interface over aggregates/entities while hiding the underlying storage mechanism.
In clean architecture, database access is an infrastructure concern in the outer layer, so swapping PostgreSQL leaves the domain and use case layers unchanged.
An aggregate is a domain-driven design concept: a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit, which is not equivalent to a database table.
A Value Object is defined by being immutable and having equality based on its field values rather than object identity.
In DDD, the aggregate root is the only member of an aggregate that external code may reference or modify, so all changes to the aggregate must pass through it.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined per aggregate root, since aggregates are the unit of persistence and access, not individual entities within them.
In Domain-Driven Design, the ubiquitous language is the common vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used consistently in code, documentation, and communication.
A context is the boundary that keeps a model and its language mutually consistent, beyond which the same words can refer to other models.
DDD advocates a rich domain model where behavior lives in the domain objects; anemic models are widely considered an anti-pattern.
A bounded context defines an explicit boundary within which a domain model applies, so the same concept (e.g., 'Customer') may be represented by different classes in different contexts.
Symfony's compiled container only instantiates a service when it is actually requested from the container, so services are lazily created by default.
The Symfony console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony autowiring automatically registers and injects services, so manual declaration for every service is not required.
Twig compiles templates into optimized PHP classes and caches them, so compilation happens only once per template instead of on every request.
In the dev environment Symfony tracks relevant files (config, classes used by the container) and only recompiles the DI container when one of them changes, otherwise it reuses the cached container.
Symfony uses the APP_ENV environment variable to determine the active environment, such as dev or prod.
Symfony's route loader and controller invocation only work with public methods, so a private method is not routable/callable as a controller action.

In Symfony, neither subscribers nor listeners have inherent priority—the execution order is determined by the priority value (in getSubscribedEvents() or the listener registration), not the interface used.
Symfony 6.0 removed the Guard authenticator system, making the authenticator-based (AuthenticatorInterface) system the only authentication mechanism.
Symfony's IsGranted attribute on a controller method enforces a role/permission and throws a 403 AccessDeniedException when it fails.

Symfony voters are indeed the mechanism used to decide whether access should be granted to a specific object, typically called via $this->isGranted('EDIT', $post) or security checks like #[IsGranted].
Symfony 7 removed the annotation loaders (e.g., from the Validator), so validation constraints must now use PHP attributes like #[Assert\NotBlank].
Symfony forms include CSRF protection by default, automatically validating the token when the form is submitted.
Symfony's validation is performed server-side on every submission, independent of any client-side HTML5 checks, which only serve as a convenience and can be bypassed.
The Symfony MakerBundle command `make:form` generates a FormType class.
Symfony stores only the user's identity (like username and roles) in the session, never the plain-text password.
In modern Symfony applications, bundle configuration is organized in config/packages with one YAML file per bundle or topic (e.g., twig.yaml, doctrine.yaml, security.yaml).
This is the standard Symfony convention: .env holds safe dev defaults and is committed, while .env.local contains real secrets and is excluded via .gitignore.
The `php bin/console debug:container` command displays all registered services and their aliases in the dependency injection container.
After compilation the container is frozen, so setParameter() is not available on the service container you get in a controller.
Since Symfony 4, services are private by default (public: false) and can only be accessed via constructor injection, not fetched directly from the container.
Bundles work with sensible default configuration; config/packages entries are optional and only needed to override defaults.
In Symfony, environment variables are referenced in services.yaml using the %env(VAR)% syntax.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable to enable debug mode, which controls the profiler and Twig debugging.
In Symfony Messenger, a single message can be handled by multiple handlers; handlers are resolved by message type, and several handlers may handle the same message class.
The sync transport handles messages immediately in the same process, without queuing them for a worker.
Symfony Messenger workers are started with the `php bin/console messenger:consume` command (often with the async transport name as an argument).
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy option is configured individually under each transport in the messenger.yaml configuration.
Symfony Messenger's default serializer uses PHP's serialize() format (PhpSerializer), not JSON; JSON is only used if you explicitly configure the Symfony Serializer with JSON format.
Symfony's Scheduler component (introduced in 6.3) produces scheduled messages that are dispatched and handled through the Messenger component.
Symfony Messenger's built-in 'doctrine' transport stores queued messages in database tables managed via Doctrine DBAL/ORM.
Custom middleware can be registered on a bus, and by disabling the default middleware you can order them freely, so they may run before or after the built-in ones.
Symfony's release schedule follows a predictable plan: major versions are released every two years, and minor versions every six months in May and November.
Symfony 8.0 requires PHP 8.4 or higher, following the same PHP version as the current Symfony 7.x line.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations, requiring native PHP attributes instead.
Symfony's AssetMapper component lets you manage and serve JavaScript and CSS directly without Node.js or webpack, using an importmap.php file to map dependencies.
Symfony 6.4 is the LTS (Long-Term Support) release of the 6.x branch, with bug fixes and security support for several years.
Symfony's upgrade policy is that deprecations added in a branch are removed in the next major version (X+1.0), so they do not keep working across majors.
Each Symfony major (and minor) release includes an UPGRADE document (e.g., UPGRADE-7.0.md) describing the changes and how to update your code.
The Symfony AssetMapper component manages JavaScript, CSS, and importmap assets natively without needing Node.js, npm, or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release at the end of November 2026, so as of 2026-11-07 it has not yet been released.
Symfony follows a six-month release cycle, so after Symfony 8.0 (November 2025) and 8.1 (May 2026), Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for November 2026.
Symfony releases a new minor version every six months, so 8.2 follows 8.1.
In Symfony's release scheme, releases like 8.2 are minor releases (Y in X.Y.Z) that maintain backward compatibility; only X.0 versions can break APIs.
PHP maintains backward compatibility within a major version, so moving from 8.1 to 8.2 should not require code changes except for rare edge cases like deprecated features.
Following Symfony's release pattern, each major branch gets minors x.0 through x.4, so 8.4 is the last minor released before Symfony 9.0.
Symfony only raises its minimum PHP requirement on major releases (like 8.0), so a minor release such as 8.2 keeps the same PHP requirement instead of requiring PHP 8.5.
Symfony keeps deprecations until the next major version, so deprecations added in the 8.x branch are only removed in Symfony 9.0.
Twig is a sandboxed template engine that only exposes explicitly registered functions, filters, and tags, so arbitrary PHP code cannot be called directly.
Twig enables HTML auto-escaping by default, so printed variables are escaped automatically.
The Twig |e filter escapes a string for safe output, defaulting to the HTML context (other strategies like js or css can be specified).
The format_number filter in twig/intl-extra uses NumberFormatter to format a number according to a given locale.
In Twig, the |raw filter marks a value as safe, so it is not auto-escaped when output.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs the value of an expression, while {% %} is used for tags that control logic such as if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the {% set %} tag.
The dump() Twig function outputs the debug information (structure and values) of a variable, typically used with the debug extension.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JavaScript library providing prebuilt UI components and styling, whereas SPA frameworks like React, Vue, or Angular handle application structure and state.
The .container class provides a responsive fixed-width container that has a set max-width at each breakpoint, while .container-fluid is full width.
The Bootstrap grid does use floats (in Bootstrap 3), but it splits a row into 12 columns, not 16.
The infixes sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl are the five named breakpoints; the default xs breakpoint uses no infix.
Bootstrap spacing utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 are calculated as multiples (or fractions) of the $spacer variable, which defaults to 1rem.
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to initialize interactive components, replacing the unprefixed data-toggle of Bootstrap 4.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and all components are written in vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the html element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM requires you to explicitly create or update the schema using the schema tool or migrations; it does not create tables automatically at runtime.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for insertion, making it managed, but the SQL INSERT is executed only when flush() is called.
In Doctrine ORM 3, EntityManager::merge() was removed (detached object merging is no longer supported), so it does not exist and cannot make an object managed.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) is an object-oriented query language that operates on entities, their fields, and associations, which Doctrine translates into SQL over underlying tables and columns.
Doctrine's find() returns null when no entity matching the given id exists.
DoctrineBundle does not flush automatically; you must explicitly call flush() on the EntityManager to persist changes.
In Doctrine ORM, entities already managed by the EntityManager are tracked by the Unit of Work, so changed properties are committed on flush() without calling persist() again.
In Doctrine, remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the actual DELETE query is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC in PostgreSQL allows readers and writers to work concurrently without blocking each other (mostly, except for DDL and exclusive locks).
The EXPLAIN command in SQL (and MySQL) shows the query execution plan without actually running the query.

Both create auto-incrementing columns backed by a sequence, but IDENTITY is the SQL-standard variant with stricter behavior (e.g., inserting explicit values requires OVERRIDING, and the column type restrictions differ from SERIAL).
In PostgreSQL, NULL values are considered distinct from each other, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL by default.
PostgreSQL's string_agg() aggregates string values into one string separated by a specified delimiter.
Plain VACUUM marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table, but only VACUUM FULL returns space to the operating system.
In a window function's OVER clause, the PARTITION BY keyword divides rows into groups (partitions) over which the function is computed.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; it still allows non-repeatable reads and phantom reads.
PostgreSQL runs each statement in its own implicit transaction and commits it immediately unless an explicit transaction (BEGIN) is started.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and permanently saves all its changes.
Indexes speed up finding rows for any query with a WHERE condition, including UPDATE and DELETE, not just SELECT.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to allow rolling back part of a transaction without aborting the whole transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to show real execution times and row counts, while plain EXPLAIN only shows the plan without running it.
The pgvector extension provides PostgreSQL with vector data types and similarity-search indexes for embeddings.
A partial index only contains entries for rows that satisfy its WHERE clause, so queries must be able to use that condition to benefit from it.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects serialization conflicts rather than locking rows that are read.
HTTP 201 (Created) indicates the request succeeded and a new resource was created.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates a successful request with no response body.
Per the HTTP specification, DELETE is idempotent: repeating the request leaves the resource in the same state (deleted).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server, not the client, to indicate which origins are permitted to access the resource.
HTTP status 429 indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given time, i.e., exceeded a rate limit.
It's reversed: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the body in both requests and responses.
RFC 5789 states PATCH is not required to be idempotent, whereas repeated PUT requests must produce the same result.
Plain == is vulnerable to timing attacks; use hash_equals() or password_verify() for constant-time comparison.
A CSRF token is generated server-side, stored in the session, embedded in forms, and verified on the server for unsafe requests like POST.
The CSP policy is enabled via the 'Content-Security-Policy' HTTP response header (X-Content-Security-Policy was a legacy variant).
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization (delegation) framework; access tokens grant access to resources and do not identify the user — authentication requires OpenID Connect.
XSS is prevented by escaping output (e.g., htmlspecialchars) when data is rendered, not merely by validating input before storing it.
The authorization server redirects to the redirect_uri with the authorization code parameter, which is then exchanged for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to request new access tokens (which are short-lived) without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
A salt does not need to be kept secret; it is typically stored alongside the hash and is only meant to prevent precomputed rainbow-table attacks, not to hide the hash.
PHPUnit only runs methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (annotated `@test` methods only work within such test classes).
setUp() runs before each test method; setUpBeforeClass() runs once before all tests.
A PHPUnit data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, causing the test to run once per data set.
The expectException() method (formerly setExpectedException()) declares that a test expects an exception of the given class to be thrown.
It's the reverse: stubs are used to return canned data, while mocks verify which methods were called.
PHPUnit 10 introduced native PHP attributes like #[DataProvider], deprecating the @dataProvider annotation (which was removed in PHPUnit 11).
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, allowing a test to receive the result of another test.
Since PHPUnit 9.2, tests run in random order when you pass the --order-by=random option on the command line.
